analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient ratios in hospitals and protects nurses who refuse unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 14, 2025 with 49 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to two House committees and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every hospital to keep a registered nurse within strict patient limits on every shift — one nurse per patient in trauma and operating rooms, up to one per four or six in less intense units. Hospitals would have to post actual staffing levels in each unit, keep records, and submit to audits. Nurses could refuse assignments that violate the limits or that they are not trained for, without being fired or reported to licensing boards, and violators would face federal fines and public listing.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would get more direct nursing attention on every shift, and registered and practical nurses, who would work under enforceable staffing limits with legal protection for refusing unsafe assignments. The bill also funds nurse scholarships, stipends, and retention grants.

how_it_helps.text: Requires hospitals to staff each unit within fixed nurse-to-patient ratios, such as one nurse per two patients in intensive care and one per four in medical-surgical units, with no averaging across shifts [S3].

Lets a nurse refuse an assignment that violates the ratios or that the nurse is not trained for, and bars hospitals from firing, retaliating, or reporting that nurse to a state licensing board; nurses who are retaliated against can sue for reinstatement, lost wages, and attorneys' fees [S3].

Requires hospitals to post actual staffing levels in each unit, keep three years of records, and makes violators' names public alongside civil fines of up to $25,000 for a first knowing violation and $50,000 for repeat violations [S3].
Adds stipends to the nurse scholarship program and expands nurse retention grants to include preceptorship and mentorship projects to keep new nurses in bedside care [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals bear the cost of hiring enough nurses to meet the ratios; Medicare payment adjustments would cover only the portion of added costs attributable to Medicare patients, so hospitals would absorb costs for other patients or try to pass them to insurers and patients. Rural hospitals get four years to comply instead of two.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, and ultimately insurers and patients

drawbacks.text: Hospitals would face large new labor costs, and Medicare adjustments cover only the Medicare-attributable share of those costs, leaving hospitals to fund compliance for commercially insured and uninsured patients themselves [S2][S3].

With a national nurse shortage already making positions hard to fill, hospitals argue fixed ratios can force unit closures, diverted ambulances, or delayed care when enough nurses cannot be hired — a cost an honest supporter must acknowledge even though the bill's findings cite studies linking California's ratios to better patient outcomes and nurse retention [S3].
Enforcement relies on HHS writing rules, conducting audits, and imposing fines, so the protections are only as strong as the administering agency chooses to make them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: fixed staffing limits mean fewer patients per nurse, which the bill's own findings say improves outcomes and nurse retention, but they cost hospitals money and can be hard to meet during a nursing shortage. The bill tries to soften this by phasing in over two to four years, exempting declared emergencies, and reimbursing hospitals for Medicare-related costs, but it would still pressure hospitals — especially small and rural ones — to find scarce nurses quickly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and split between two House committees, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on May 14, 2025 [S1][S5].
The Speaker referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, each for the parts within its jurisdiction [S1][S5].
Forty-nine House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors as of the bill's cosponsor page [S4].
The action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor action after the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, hospital operators, who avoid a federal staffing mandate and its labor costs while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set federal hospital nurse-to-patient ratios and nurse refusal protections.

for.name: National Nurses United and nurses' unions
for.what_they_did: Long pushed federal staffing-ratio legislation and backing for nurses who refuse unsafe assignments; this bill builds on that campaign.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: One of two committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 14, 2025 and has taken no further action on the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 14, 2025 and has taken no further action on the bill.

against.name: American Hospital Association and hospital industry
against.what_they_did: Have opposed federal one-size-fits-all nurse staffing mandates, arguing hospitals should set staffing by patient acuity and that rigid ratios are unworkable during nurse shortages.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republicans signed on, and both committees where the bill sits are controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: Hospitals would have to hire many more direct-care nurses, post ratios, keep three years of records, face audits and fines, and publish violators' names; Medicare payment adjustments cover only the Medicare-attributable share of the added cost. Hospitals have pushed back against federal ratios for years because staffing is their largest controllable expense.

The bill does not ban agency nurses but bars hospitals from using temporary staff who have not demonstrated competence on the assigned unit and received orientation, which could reduce use of expensive agency labor while raising its quality.

analysis.trajectory: Bills sent to two committees with no Republican cosponsors rarely reach the House floor; unless a committee schedules a markup, this bill is likely to sit without action until the Congress ends, as earlier versions of similar nurse-ratio bills have.
